Trisha, you're chewing your nails over this band audition, so let your Deepika Maasi tell you something.

When I was fifteen, our school started a band. They needed a drummer. I had been drumming on every tiffin box and table in Pune for years. Everyone told me to go.

And I said, very calmly, "I'll fail." I could see it: my sticks slipping, the music teacher frowning, the older boys smirking at a girl on drums. It didn't feel like a fear. It felt like I already knew, the way you know tomorrow is Tuesday.

So I didn't go. I sat at home and polished my shoes, of all things.

Two years later, at my farewell, the music teacher said, "Why didn't you ever try for the band? We never found a decent drummer."

I never found out if I'd fail. That's the part that still pinches. The forecast was the only thing that actually stopped me.

qa.a: She sat at home and polished her shoes.

qa.q: Why did "I'll fail" feel like knowledge to fifteen-year-old Deepika?
qa.a: She could picture the whole scene so clearly, the sticks slipping and the frowns, that it felt as certain as the day of the week. Picturing it vividly made the guess feel like a fact.

qa.q: What turning point is Deepika Maasi hoping Trisha will choose differently?
qa.a: Deepika is hoping Trisha goes to the audition despite the forecast, since staying home is the only way to be sure of never finding out. Going gives the prediction a chance to be proved wrong.

qa.q: How might the music teacher's words at the farewell have felt to Deepika?
qa.a: They probably stung, showing that the chance had been real all along. Hearing the band never found a decent drummer turned the old forecast into a regret.

Teacher's note, inter-school debate selection, 3 August.

Pankaj did not come to today's selection round. Yesterday he told me, very calmly, "I'll definitely fail. The seniors will destroy me, and I'll freeze on the first point." He said it as if it had already happened.

This worries me, because in class he argues clearly and with good examples. He has never actually been tested in a selection round, so his forecast rests on fear, not results.

After school I spoke to him. I asked him to rate, from zero to a hundred, how sure he was that he'd fail. He said ninety. I asked what evidence he had. He listed feelings, not facts. I have offered him a place in Friday's practice round: low stakes, only three judges. He agreed to come, and to write down his prediction first so we can compare afterwards.

Gargi, English department

qa.a: Pankaj said ninety, out of a hundred.

qa.a: Pankaj feels anxious about the seniors and about freezing, and the fear is so strong that failure seems already certain.

qa.a: A low-stakes practice round with Pankaj writing his prediction first, so the real result can test the forecast.

qa.q: How might the judges see Pankaj if he comes on Friday?

Ramesh
